title: Feds Got Warrants to Use Fake Cell Towers to Hunt Down Don Lemon’s Producer
gist: Court filings show federal agents obtained warrants to use cell-site simulators (Stingrays) to locate a student producer for journalist Don Lemon charged over a St. Paul church anti-ICE protest. The affidavits contained a false claim, DHS used customs summonses against journalists, and critics question whether such intrusive tools were necessary.

themes.theme: Cell-site simulator warrants against protest figures

insights.claim: Judges in Minnesota and Pennsylvania signed warrants on January 30 and 31 authorizing cell-site simulators to locate Jerome Richardson, a Temple University student who helped produce Don Lemon's coverage, and he surrendered voluntarily two days after the second warrant.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Shows intrusive surveillance tech being applied to a low-flight-risk protest defendant, relevant to the political and legal risk around surveillance vendors.

insights.claim: Agents also applied for simulator warrants targeting journalist Georgia Fort and Jamael Lundy and sought pen register orders on Fort and a number traced to Lemon, but the records do not show whether the applications were approved or whether a simulator was actually used.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Uncertainty about deployment is itself notable, as even prosecutors reportedly did not know if the surveillance yielded evidence.
insights.locator: Agents also applied for cell-site simulator warrants

insights.claim: Cell-site simulators impersonate cell towers and also collect identifying data from any nearby phone, including those of people not suspected of crimes, which privacy advocates call dragnet surveillance.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Bystander-collection design drives the legal and policy risk for these devices.
insights.locator: Cell-site simulators impersonate cell phone towers

insights.claim: EFF's Cooper Quintin calls using such a tool on the press for stories unfavorable to the president an appalling attack on the First Amendment; WIRED also found EFF-software evidence of a simulator near the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, operator unknown.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Civil-liberties pushback and detection tooling raise the chance of litigation and regulation of surveillance devices.
insights.quote: Using an advanced surveillance capability such as a cell-site simulator against members of the free press

insights.claim: Police borrowing FBI simulators had to agree to keep details of their use secret, even in court, according to FBI records released in 2023.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Secrecy requirements limit judicial oversight and make deployment hard to audit.
insights.locator: The use of cell-site simulators has long been shrouded in secrecy

themes.theme: Questionable government conduct in the case

insights.claim: Prosecutors conceded Lemon and Fort did not chant, yet the claim they were chanting with agitators appeared in at least 15 warrant affidavits, raising questions about the accuracy of what judges were told.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Inaccurate affidavits could lead to suppression of evidence and weaken the cases.

insights.claim: DHS demanded journalists' phone and YouTube records under a customs authority needing no prior judicial approval, and sought records of everyone who bought a particular REI beanie in the Twin Cities over more than two years; defense lawyers have identified 92 customs summonses.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Shows broad use of administrative subpoenas to collect data on private firms' customers, a compliance risk for retailers and platforms such as YouTube.

insights.claim: A magistrate refused five of eight arrest warrants, two for a journalist and his producer with no evidence of criminal behavior, and the Justice Department withdrew after an appeals court rejected its override bid, before securing a grand jury indictment on January 29.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Judicial resistance and a switch to the grand jury route show how the government worked around courts.

insights.claim: A former counterterrorism prosecutor said using a simulator to locate someone is not necessarily unusual but called the tactics here aggressive and unnecessary.
insights.speaker: Dhruv Mehrotra
insights.so_what: Practitioner skepticism suggests the tool was used beyond normal need.
insights.quote: I don’t understand why it would be at all necessary.
